one_line: New York public-hospital leader who became KP Southern California regional president and drove a fast-moving quality era
top_role: Regional President, Kaiser Foundation Health Plan and Hospitals, Southern California

journey.year_note: He says only 'in the 1950s' and 'at the age of three'.
journey.label: Hospitalized child given pediatrician's stethoscope
journey.fortune_basis: she was just a lovely, lovely person
journey.quote: one of the things she did was she gave me an old stethoscope of hers. Right. So my mother saw it and she said, oh, he's going to be a doctor.

journey.year_note: Later in the interview he dates the medical clinic years as '82 to 85'.
journey.label: Takes on Kings County medical clinic
journey.fortune_basis: we did reorganize it. We got into some reasonably good shape.
journey.quote: when I finished my chief residency, I talked my chair into letting me run the medical clinic at Kings County Hospital. And that was because it was sort of a disastrous, chaotic place.

journey.year_note: He places it both in 'the early 80s' and between 1985 and 1989, so no single year.
journey.label: Runs Kings County ER, burns out
journey.fortune_basis: I just realized I was, I was burning out
journey.quote: I took over the Kings County emergency room, not because I wanted to become an ER doctor or run an ER, it was because it was so badly run

journey.year_note: He finished his MPH in 1989, then went to Washington, and came back in 1990.
journey.label: Health policy fellow for Senator Bradley
journey.fortune_basis: getting to work for a childhood sports hero was incredible
journey.quote: I applied for what was called the Robert Wood Johnson Health Policy Fellowship, it's in Washington, DC

journey.label: Chief medical officer, NYC public hospitals
journey.fortune_basis: that administration was so incompetent that I was the go to person
journey.quote: I got a call and said, would you like to be the chief medical officer here at the corporate headquarters? And so I said, yes, I did.

journey.year_note: He became CMO in 1990 and was there 'almost four years' before the mayor changed; an 'eight year hiatus' then ran to 2002.
journey.label: Leaves when mayoralty changes hands
journey.fortune_basis: He wanted to sell everything or give it to the private sector.
journey.quote: David Dinkins lost the mayoral election to Rudy Giuliani, and I just could not stand Rudy Giuliani, just to be honest with you.

journey.label: President of NYC Health and Hospitals
journey.fortune_basis: that was the high point of my career in New York City
journey.quote: Mike Bloomberg, you know, who really believes in meritocracy, right? He, um, he reached out, I interviewed and, uh, unbelievably, unbelievable to me, he offered me the job.

journey.year_note: The lesson comes from working for Bloomberg as HHC president, 2002 to 2005.
journey.label: Learns reflected glory from Bloomberg
journey.fortune_basis: So it was an incredibly valuable lesson. I loved working for Mike Bloomberg.
journey.quote: if you're in a leadership position, reflected glory is sometimes better than direct glory

journey.label: Recruited as KP Southern California president
journey.fortune_basis: the interview part process, I have to tell you was torturous
journey.quote: the Kaiser Permanente was not used to having a physician on the health plan hospital side

journey.year_note: Describes his first months after arriving in 2005.
journey.label: Partnership with Jeff Weisz on quality
journey.fortune_basis: immediately we clicked. I mean, it was amazing.
journey.quote: he and I and Mike Kanter, at that time, we just all embraced the quality agenda.

journey.year_note: 'In the first year I was there', after arriving in 2005; could be 2005 or 2006.
journey.label: Fights for a $15 million project
journey.fortune_basis: George gave me a hard time, believe it or not
journey.quote: Well, because I was new and Jeff was cantankerous at the time. Um, the, uh, people who were approving these projects told George that, you know, Jeff was railroading this thing

journey.year_note: Undated; he places it when the region had about 3 million members.
journey.label: Pushes Medicaid growth: 'Ben's kids'
journey.fortune_basis: so I, I, I'm actually very proud of that.
journey.quote: I said, Jeff, we got to do more Medicaid, we got to do more Medicaid, and he, um, he, to his credit, he listened to me

journey.year_note: Describes the span of his tenure, 2005 to 2016, as a whole.
journey.label: A golden period of growth
journey.fortune_basis: it was a golden period for us
journey.quote: it was a golden period for us, I think, where, you know, it was just, uh, an upward spiral, right. Better quality, better care, better patient engagement, uh, better growth, more money

journey.label: Medical school finally gains traction
journey.fortune_basis: So it was a labor of love, took a long time.
journey.quote: it was only until, uh, Bernard came in, I think it was probably 2013 that we had some traction on medical school.

journey.label: Leaves KP for Texas
journey.fortune_basis: Didn't quite work out the way I wanted it to
journey.quote: I left in 2016 to go to Texas of all places because I wanted to see what I could do with a, you know, a regular system

journey.label: Consults, then retires
journey.quote: I came back to New York, where I was a consultant for a while, and during Covid, I retired. But I have to say that it was an incredible career

events.name: 1990s KP national expansion
events.view: He thinks the 1990s expansion failed because Permanente did not back it, partners lacked managed-care experience and membership was too small.
events.quote: the reason why I think the, the 90s, um, expansion failed, number one, there was a lot of, um, a lot of consternation amongst the Permanente Medical Group.

prompt.question: So when KP expanded to New York, what was your role In New York... And then the other question is, why did it fail so quickly?

events.year_note: He says "the 90s, um, expansion"; a decade, not a stated year.

events.name: 1990s financial crisis
events.view: He recalls KP nearly going bankrupt in the late 1990s and thinks the turmoil left leaders skittish and slow to act.
events.quote: we had three days of cash on hand at one point and really was a whole a bunch of stuff that saved Kaiser Permanente in the late 90s

prompt.question: So did you actually make that decision just to clarify during your residency that, you know, like you're going to go more in an administrative leadership track versus a clinical track?

events.name: PACS digital radiology rollout
events.view: He pushed a fast, region-wide $100 million PACS rollout and saw it win the trust of Permanente physicians.
events.quote: But this was 2005, right? And believe it or not, in the public hospital systems, one of the things I did was I put a PAC system in place.

prompt.question: So did you actually make that decision just to clarify during your residency that, you know, like you're going to go more in an administrative leadership track versus a clinical track?

events.name: POINT population care tool
events.view: He credits Southern California's POINT real-time data tool for closing care gaps, later adopted program-wide as CarePoint.
events.quote: the Permanente Medical Group had developed this, uh, the system called POINT, the Permanente Online Interactive Network Tool

prompt.question: So did you actually make that decision just to clarify during your residency that, you know, like you're going to go more in an administrative leadership track versus a clinical track?

events.name: Seismic hospital rebuild
events.view: He prioritized rebuilding hospitals to meet California earthquake standards, then ambulatory sites, and says it came in cheaper than Northern California.
events.quote: We rebuilt our hospitals. We decided that, you know, because of the earthquake standards that came into play in, in California, that we had to build those hospitals

prompt.question: So did you actually make that decision just to clarify during your residency that, you know, like you're going to go more in an administrative leadership track versus a clinical track?

events.name: Electronic health record rollout
events.view: He says Southern California compressed Epic's three implementation phases into two, a process he says Epic still uses.
events.quote: we're going to merge two of these phases. So we actually invented a process that in Southern California that Epic uses now

prompt.question: what were the aspects of Permanente medicine that kind of surprised you or you were unaware of until you experienced them firsthand?

events.name: Electronic health record rollout
events.view: He credits George Halvorson with the decision for a unified Epic system despite opposition, and calls it right.
events.quote: the decision to go with Epic was really George's decision, you know, to have a unified system, and it was not without opposition.

prompt.question: an example of one of the big projects of the time, of course, was working and deciding on epic versus Cerner or whoever, and then rolling it out.

events.name: Affordable Care Act
events.view: He saw the ACA as good for KP, driving rapid Southern California growth that was hard to absorb.
events.quote: it helped propel some of the growth for us in, in Southern California, particularly after I think it was 2014 was when the enrollment started.

prompt.question: I think it would be great if you could summarize what Affordable Care Act was, how it affected Kaiser Permanente

events.name: Medicaid expansion
events.view: He pushed KP Southern California to take far more Medicaid members, controversial for finances but which he calls mission and his legacy.
events.quote: they used to call them Ben's kids. That's what they called it. Right. But it was the right thing to do.

prompt.question: I think it would be great if you could summarize what Affordable Care Act was, how it affected Kaiser Permanente

events.name: KP School of Medicine founded
events.view: He backed the medical school from its first proposal around 2006 and says it only gained traction once Bernard Tyson led.
events.quote: It was maybe 2006 or 7 when Jeff and Mike Kantor came to me and said, uh, why we want to start a medical school, right, would you support it?

prompt.question: tell us a little bit on another topic, um, about your thoughts and your support for the School of Medicine when you first heard about it.

events.name: Tahoe agreement
events.year_note: Year from the interviewer: "1955 Tahoe agreement"
events.view: He sees the Tahoe agreement as the clear division of responsibilities behind good partnerships, but one that does not flex for expansion.
events.quote: partially because I think the Tahoe agreement made it clear whose responsibilities were what, right.

prompt.question: what advantages Kaiser Permanente's integrated partnership health plan hospitals. Medical group the traditional KP. 1955 Tahoe agreement have over organizations

events.name: KP Medical Foundation formed
events.view: He sees the foundation model as working closer with the health plan and moving faster, at a possible cost to Permanente innovation.
events.quote: once you become so close to the, the, the health plan hospital, you might lose some of the innovation, right.

prompt.question: what do you see as the advantages and disadvantages of the new Medical Foundation model? You know, with Washington, Colorado, um, versus the traditional integrated federation model

events.name: Risant Health formed
events.view: As a Geisinger and Cone Health board member, he sees Risant as unlike the 1990s expansion because it joins whole, established health systems.
events.quote: the situation is very different, right? Because, you know, the, the Risant is, is, um, an organization that has completely formed health center health system

prompt.question: So can you contrast that with what's going on today with recent, you know, and, and the expansion?

events.name: KP Reno expansion
events.view: He understands Reno went a different way from Risant because the hospital system declined, with TPMG helping the local medical group.
events.quote: Northern California Permanente Medical Group, um, really were given the charge to come and help the medical group in, in Reno, um, develop more like a Permanente Medical Group.

prompt.question: why was KP Reno, KP Reno versus resent Reno, you know, with the doctors there? What was the decision?

retellable.title: The $100 million back-of-envelope PACS decision
retellable.summary: In 2005, when Southern California radiology said it could not afford digital imaging, Chu asked what a system-wide rollout would cost and approved $100 million on the spot. The fast rollout helped win over Permanente physicians.
retellable.quote: So I said, could we do it for $100 million? So he said, um, yeah, I guess we could do it for $100 million. I said, okay, do it.
retellable.why: Shows decisive health plan leadership earning physician trust.

retellable.title: "Ben's kids": the case for Medicaid
retellable.summary: Chu showed Jeff Weisz that falling family size meant fewer child members, so KP would either cut pediatricians or take more Medicaid children. Colleagues came to call the new members 'Ben's kids'.
retellable.quote: So I said, Jeff, are you going to fire 15%, 20% of your pediatricians? I said, you know, if you if you're not going to do that, we're going to have to increase the numbers
retellable.why: Mission argued through hard numbers; a memorable label for equity work.

retellable.title: How POINT became CarePoint
retellable.summary: After Epic went in, George Halvorson complained KP lacked real-time quality data, and for over a year Chu kept pointing to Southern California's POINT tool. Once SoCal's scores led the program, IT adopted it nationally as CarePoint.
retellable.quote: every time he said that, I raised my hand and said, we do in Southern California, we have the point system.
retellable.why: Shows results, not argument, spreading a regional innovation program-wide.

retellable.title: A pediatrician's old stethoscope
retellable.summary: Hospitalized for months at age three with rheumatic fever, Chu was given an old stethoscope by his pediatrician. His mother declared he would be a doctor.
retellable.quote: one of the things she did was she gave me an old stethoscope of hers. Right. So my mother saw it and she said, oh, he's going to be a doctor. He's going to be a doctor.
retellable.why: A vivid origin story about how one clinician's kindness shapes a career.

questions_that_opened_things_up.why: Drew his story of threatening to quit to save public-hospital EHR funding.
